question: What is the median of the values 4, 8, 6, 5, 3, 10?
explanation: Sorted: 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10; with an even count the median is the average of the 3rd and 4th values, (5+6)/2 = 5.5. The value 6.0 is the arithmetic mean, not the median.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Median

question: Five values have a mean of 10. A sixth value, 22, is added. What is the new mean?
explanation: The sum was 50; adding 22 gives 72, and 72/6 = 12. Averaging 10 and 22 (giving 16) ignores the different numbers of observations behind each figure.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Average

question: Group A (40 % of staff) has an average salary of 50 and group B (60 %) has 80. What is the overall average salary?
explanation: Weighted mean = 0.4 × 50 + 0.6 × 80 = 20 + 48 = 68. The simple mean of the two group averages (65) ignores the group sizes.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Weighted average

question: Every value in a dataset is multiplied by 3. What happens to the standard deviation?
explanation: Standard deviation is expressed in the units of the data and scales linearly with a multiplicative factor; only the variance is multiplied by 9. Adding a constant, by contrast, would leave it unchanged.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Standard deviation

question: What is the sample variance (divisor n − 1) of the values 2, 4, 6?
explanation: Mean = 4; squared deviations are 4, 0, 4, summing to 8; 8/(3−1) = 4. The figure 2.67 results from dividing by n, which gives the population variance.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Standard deviation

question: Tukey's rule flags values beyond 1.5 × IQR from the quartiles. With Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 36, which observation is flagged as an upper outlier?
explanation: IQR = 16, so the upper fence is 36 + 1.5 × 16 = 60. Only 64 lies beyond it; the others are below 60.

source.title: Data Visualisation Guide (Publications Office, data.europa.eu), Box plots (quartiles, whiskers, 1.5 × IQR outlier rule)

question: In a distribution the mean is clearly larger than the median. Which description is most likely?
explanation: A long right tail pulls the mean upward while the median stays near the bulk of the data. In a left-skewed distribution the mean falls below the median.

source.title: Data Visualisation Guide (Publications Office, data.europa.eu), The mean versus the median

question: A value of 130 comes from a distribution with mean 100 and standard deviation 15. What is its z-score?
explanation: z = (130 − 100)/15 = 2.0, i.e. two standard deviations above the mean. The value 30 is the raw difference, not standardised.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Standard deviation (basis of standardisation and z-scores)

question: A price index (2015 = 100) shows 125 in 2020 and 150 in 2024. What is the 2024 value when the index is rebased to 2020 = 100?
explanation: Rebasing divides by the new base value: 150/125 × 100 = 120. Simply subtracting 25 points would give 125, which ignores that the base changed proportionally.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Index number

question: A value rises by 20 % and then falls by 20 %. How does the final value compare with the start?
explanation: 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96, so the final value is 4 % below the start. Percentage changes are applied to different bases and do not cancel out.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Percentage change

question: The unemployment rate rises from 5 % to 6 %. Which statement is correct?
options: It rose by 20 percentage points, or 1 % in relative terms
It rose by 1 percentage point, or 1 % in relative terms
It rose by 1 percentage point, or 20 % in relative terms
It rose by 1 %, or 20 percentage points
explanation: The absolute difference of rates is expressed in percentage points (6 − 5 = 1); the relative change is 1/5 = 20 %. Mixing the two units is a common reporting error.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Percentage point

question: A series grows by 10 % in year 1 and 20 % in year 2. Compared with 15 %, its average annual growth rate (geometric) is:
options: Cannot be compared without absolute levels
explanation: The geometric average is √(1.10 × 1.20) − 1 = √1.32 − 1 ≈ 14.9 %. The arithmetic mean of growth rates (15 %) overstates compound growth.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Geometric mean

question: A frequency table shows value 1 (5 cases), 2 (8), 3 (4), 4 (3). What is the median?
explanation: With n = 20 the median lies between the 10th and 11th ordered values; cumulative counts are 5, 13, … so both are 2. The value 2.25 is the mean.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Median

question: Which chart type is best suited to show the distribution of a continuous variable such as household income?
explanation: A histogram groups a continuous variable into adjacent classes and shows its shape. A pie chart shows shares of a whole, and a line chart shows development over time.

source.title: Data Visualisation Guide (Publications Office, data.europa.eu), Histograms (background; the area rule for unequal bins is general statistics practice)

question: A bar chart compares two values (98 and 102) using a y-axis starting at 96. What is the main problem?
options: The values are too close to compare
The bars should be replaced by a pie chart
The truncated axis exaggerates the difference
Bar charts cannot show two values
explanation: Bars encode value by length, so a non-zero baseline distorts the ratio: with the axis starting at 96 the bars measure 2 and 6, so a 4 % difference looks threefold. Bar charts should normally start at zero.

source.title: Data Visualisation Guide (Publications Office, data.europa.eu), Starting bars at zero

question: Why is a 3D pie chart with 12 slices considered poor practice?
options: Twelve slices always sum to more than 100 %
Perspective and many slices distort and hinder comparison of shares
explanation: Human perception compares angles and areas poorly, and 3D perspective enlarges front slices. A sorted bar chart communicates the same shares more accurately.

source.title: Data Visualisation Guide (Publications Office, data.europa.eu), Guidelines for pie charts

question: An indicator has mean 40 and standard deviation 6. What is its coefficient of variation?
explanation: CV = SD/mean = 6/40 = 0.15 = 15 %. Being unit-free, it allows comparing the variability of variables measured on different scales.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Coefficient of variation

question: Country A has a labour force of 10 million and unemployment of 4 %; country B has 30 million and 8 %. What is the combined unemployment rate?
explanation: Unemployed: 0.4 + 2.4 = 2.8 million out of 40 million = 7 %. The simple average (6 %) ignores the very different labour-force weights.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Weighted average

question: A histogram has unequal class widths. To represent frequencies correctly, which element must be proportional to the frequency?
explanation: With unequal classes, height would mislead; bar area (height × width) must correspond to frequency, so height shows density. With equal widths, height and area are interchangeable.

source.title: Data Visualisation Guide (Publications Office, data.europa.eu), Histograms (background; the area rule for unequal bins is general statistics practice)

question: In a dataset of more than two values, the largest value is replaced by a far larger value. Which measure remains unchanged?
explanation: The median depends only on the middle position of the ordered data, so it is robust to extreme values. Mean, range and standard deviation all change.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Median

question: Q1 = 12 and Q3 = 30. What is the interquartile range?
explanation: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 30 − 12 = 18. It measures the spread of the central 50 % of observations.

source.title: Data Visualisation Guide (Publications Office, data.europa.eu), Box plots (quartiles, whiskers, 1.5 × IQR outlier rule)

question: What distinguishes a Laspeyres price index from a Paasche price index?
options: Laspeyres weights prices by base-period quantities
Laspeyres is a geometric mean of both
explanation: A Laspeyres index prices the fixed base-period basket in the current period, while Paasche uses current-period quantities. The geometric mean of the two is the Fisher index.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Index number (general index concept; Laspeyres/Paasche weighting is standard index theory)

question: A vehicle drives out at 60 km/h and returns at 40 km/h over the same road. What is the average speed for the round trip?
explanation: Average speed is total distance over total time, i.e. the harmonic mean: 2/(1/60 + 1/40) = 48. The arithmetic mean (50) wrongly weights by time rather than distance.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Average

question: After standardising a variable to z-scores, what are its mean and standard deviation?
explanation: Subtracting the mean centres the data at 0 and dividing by the standard deviation scales the spread to 1.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Standard deviation (basis of standardisation and z-scores)

question: A region is at the 90th percentile of an income distribution. What does this mean?
options: About 90 % of regions have an income at or below it
Its income is 90 % of the mean
It has 90 % of the total income
It is 90 units above the median
explanation: The p-th percentile is the value below which (about) p % of observations fall. It says nothing about shares of total income.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Median (the 50th percentile; other percentiles generalise it)

question: On a logarithmic y-axis, equal vertical distances between points represent equal:
explanation: On a log scale, a constant slope means a constant growth rate, so equal distances correspond to equal ratios. On a linear axis, equal distances represent equal differences.

source.title: Data Visualisation Guide (Publications Office, data.europa.eu), Logarithmic y axes

question: In a stacked bar chart with four segments, which comparison is hardest for readers?
options: The size of a middle segment across different bars
The size of the bottom segment across bars
The total height of each bar
The ranking of the bar totals
explanation: Only the bottom segment and the total share a common baseline; middle segments float, so their lengths cannot be compared easily. Grouped bars or small multiples avoid this.

source.title: Data Visualisation Guide (Publications Office, data.europa.eu), Stacked bars

question: Nominal wages rise by 21 % while consumer prices rise by 10 %. By how much do real wages rise?
explanation: Real growth is 1.21/1.10 − 1 = 10 %. Subtracting 10 points gives 11 %, which is only an approximation that works for small rates.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Inflation (inflation rate as percentage change of a price index)

question: 5 units have a mean of 2,000 and 15 units have a mean of 3,000. What is the mean of all 20 units?
explanation: (5 × 2,000 + 15 × 3,000)/20 = 55,000/20 = 2,750. The unweighted average of the group means (2,500) is wrong because the groups differ in size.

source.title: Data Visualisation Guide (Publications Office, data.europa.eu), The mean versus the median

question: In a box plot the median line sits close to Q1 and the upper whisker is much longer than the lower one. What does this suggest?
explanation: A median near the lower quartile combined with a long upper tail indicates positive (right) skew. Box plots cannot reliably reveal bimodality.

source.title: Data Visualisation Guide (Publications Office, data.europa.eu), Box plots (quartiles, whiskers, 1.5 × IQR outlier rule)

question: P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A and B) = 0.1. What is P(A or B)?
explanation: P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B) = 0.3 + 0.4 − 0.1 = 0.6. Adding without subtracting the overlap (0.7) double-counts it.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: Events A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.2. What is P(A and B)?
explanation: For independent events P(A∩B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.1. The value 0.70 is the sum, which would apply to disjoint events' union.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: P(A and B) = 0.12 and P(B) = 0.40. What is P(A | B)?
explanation: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) = 0.12/0.40 = 0.30. Conditioning restricts the sample space to B, so we divide by P(B).

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: A disease has 1 % prevalence. A test has 90 % sensitivity and a 9 % false-positive rate. About what share of positive results are true cases?
explanation: True positives 0.009; false positives 0.99 × 0.09 = 0.0891; P(D|+) = 0.009/0.0981 ≈ 9.2 %. Ignoring the low base rate leads to the 90 % misreading.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: A fair coin is tossed 4 times. What is the probability of exactly 2 heads?
explanation: Binomial: C(4,2) × 0.5⁴ = 6/16 = 0.375. The value 0.5 confuses 'exactly 2' with the expected proportion of heads.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: X is binomial with n = 100 and p = 0.2. What are its mean and variance?
explanation: Mean = np = 20 and variance = np(1−p) = 16. Mean equal to variance characterises the Poisson distribution.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: For a Poisson-distributed count with mean 3, what is the variance?
explanation: A Poisson distribution has variance equal to its mean (λ). Equidispersion is the property tested when checking for overdispersion in count data.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: IQ scores are approximately normal with mean 100 and SD 15. Roughly what share lies between 70 and 130?
explanation: 70 and 130 are ±2 SD from the mean, which covers about 95 % of a normal distribution. ±1 SD covers about 68 % and ±3 SD about 99.7 %.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: What does the central limit theorem state?
options: Every population becomes normal as it grows
Means of large random samples are approximately normally distributed
Sample means equal the population mean
explanation: For independent observations with finite variance, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normality as n grows, whatever the population shape. It does not make the population itself normal.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: The population SD is 20 and the sample size is 100. What is the standard error of the sample mean?
explanation: SE = σ/√n = 20/10 = 2. Using the SD itself (20) ignores that averaging reduces variability.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: The sample size is multiplied by 4, everything else equal. What happens to the standard error of the mean?
explanation: SE is proportional to 1/√n, so quadrupling n halves it. Quartering the error would need 16 times the sample.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: A sample mean is 50 with standard error 2. What is the approximate 95 % confidence interval?
explanation: 50 ± 1.96 × 2 = 50 ± 3.92, giving 46.1 to 53.9. The range 48–52 is ±1 SE, a confidence level of only about 68 %.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: Which interpretation of a 95 % confidence interval is correct?
options: The estimate is correct with probability 0.95
There is a 95 % chance the true value lies in this particular interval
95 % of the observations lie in the interval
If the procedure were repeated, about 95 % of such intervals would contain the true parameter
explanation: Confidence refers to the long-run coverage of the procedure; a given interval either contains the parameter or not. The probability reading belongs to Bayesian credible intervals.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: What does a p-value measure?
options: The probability that the result is due to chance alone
The probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming H0 is true
The probability that H0 is true
The probability that H1 is true
explanation: The p-value is computed under the assumption that the null hypothesis holds; it is not the probability of the hypothesis itself. Treating it as P(H0) is a classic misinterpretation.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: What is a type I error?
options: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
explanation: A type I error is a false positive whose probability is the significance level α. Failing to reject a false null is a type II error.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: If the probability of a type II error is β = 0.2, what is the power of the test?
explanation: Power = 1 − β = 0.80, the probability of rejecting a false null hypothesis. The value 0.95 relates to 1 − α.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: Which change increases the power of a test, other things equal?
explanation: More observations reduce the standard error and make a given effect easier to detect. Lowering α, larger variance or smaller effects all reduce power.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: Mean income is to be compared across three independent regions. Which test is appropriate?
explanation: ANOVA tests equality of more than two group means; repeated pairwise t-tests inflate the type I error. Chi-square suits categorical variables.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: Which test examines whether two categorical variables (e.g. region and employment status) are associated?
explanation: The chi-square test compares observed with expected counts in a contingency table. The t-test and ANOVA compare means of numeric variables.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: Employees' test scores are recorded before and after training. Which test is most appropriate to assess the mean change?
explanation: Before and after values come from the same units and are dependent, so the differences are analysed with a paired t-test. An independent test ignores that pairing and loses power.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: Which design best describes stratified random sampling?
options: Every k-th unit is selected from a list
The population is split into homogeneous groups and each is sampled randomly
Whole groups are selected at random and fully surveyed
Volunteers are accepted until a quota is met
explanation: Stratification samples within every stratum, which ensures representation and usually improves precision. Selecting whole groups describes cluster sampling.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Stratum

question: For the same sample size, cluster sampling typically yields estimates that are:
options: Equally precise, as selection is random
Unbiased and exact for any cluster size
More precise, because clusters are homogeneous
Less precise than simple random sampling, because units in a cluster are similar
explanation: Intra-cluster correlation raises variance (the design effect exceeds 1). Cluster sampling is chosen for lower fieldwork cost, not for precision.

source.title: ESS Handbook for Quality and Metadata Reports (2021), accuracy: sampling and non-sampling errors

question: A list holds 1,200 units and a systematic sample of 60 is needed. What is the sampling interval?
explanation: The interval is k = N/n = 1,200/60 = 20, with a random start between 1 and 20. Periodicity in the list is the main risk of this design.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Sample survey (general background on sampling)

question: Unit non-response in a survey is most problematic when:
options: The frame is up to date
Respondents and non-respondents differ on the variable of interest
explanation: Non-response creates bias only if non-respondents systematically differ from respondents. A low rate alone does not prove bias, nor does a high rate rule it out.

source.title: ESS Handbook for Quality and Metadata Reports (2021), accuracy: sampling and non-sampling errors

question: A unit is selected with inclusion probability 1/50. What is its design weight?
explanation: The design weight is the inverse of the inclusion probability: 1/(1/50) = 50, i.e. the unit represents 50 population units.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Weight

question: A sampling frame omits people living in new buildings. Which error results?
explanation: Units missing from the frame have no chance of selection, so estimates can be biased regardless of sample size. This is a non-sampling error.

source.title: ESS Handbook for Quality and Metadata Reports (2021), accuracy: sampling and non-sampling errors

question: According to the ESS guidelines, which components does a seasonally adjusted series contain?
explanation: Seasonal adjustment removes seasonal (and, where relevant, calendar) effects, leaving trend-cycle plus irregular. Adding back seasonality gives the unadjusted series.

source.title: Eurostat, ESS guidelines on seasonal adjustment (2015 edition)

question: What does calendar adjustment of a monthly series correct for?
options: Differences in working days and moving holidays such as Easter
explanation: Calendar adjustment removes the effect of varying trading days and moving holidays. Removing price effects is deflation.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Calendar adjustment

question: Twenty independent hypothesis tests are run at α = 0.05 and all null hypotheses are true. How many significant results are expected by chance?
explanation: Expected false positives = 20 × 0.05 = 1. Without a multiple-testing correction, the chance of at least one is 1 − 0.95²⁰ ≈ 64 %.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: For a proportion p = 0.5 and n = 400, what is the approximate 95 % margin of error?
explanation: SE = √(0.25/400) = 0.025; margin = 1.96 × 0.025 ≈ 0.049. The value ±2.5 is one standard error only.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: Strata contain 600 and 400 units. With proportional allocation of n = 100, how many units come from each stratum?
explanation: Proportional allocation matches sample shares to population shares: 100 × 0.6 and 100 × 0.4. Equal allocation gives 50 and 50.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Stratum

question: A game pays 10 with probability 0.2 and costs 3 with probability 0.8. What is the expected gain per play?
explanation: E = 0.2 × 10 − 0.8 × 3 = 2 − 2.4 = −0.4. The values +2.0 and −2.4 each take only one branch of the outcomes.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: With a very large sample, a tiny difference becomes statistically significant. What follows?
options: The null hypothesis is certainly false in practice
Significance does not imply the effect is practically relevant
explanation: Statistical significance reflects detectability, which grows with n; the effect size and its confidence interval decide relevance. A small p-value does not measure magnitude.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: Three independent events each have probability 0.1. What is the probability that at least one occurs?
explanation: 1 − 0.9³ = 1 − 0.729 = 0.271. The sum 0.3 ignores the overlap, and 0.729 is the probability that none occurs.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: A two-sided z-test gives z = 2.1 at α = 0.05. What is the conclusion?
options: Do not reject H0, since z is above 0
Do not reject H0, since z is below 2.58
explanation: The two-sided 5 % critical value is 1.96; 2.1 exceeds it (p ≈ 0.036). At α = 0.01 the critical value 2.58 would not be exceeded.

source.title: Standard textbook result without an official EU definition; related concept: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Estimator

question: Ice-cream sales and drowning incidents are strongly correlated across months. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The correlation must be a coding error
A confounder, such as hot weather, drives both
explanation: Correlation does not establish causation; a common cause (temperature) can produce association between unrelated outcomes. Causal claims need design or adjustment.

source.title: Data Visualisation Guide (Publications Office, data.europa.eu), Correlation is not causation

question: What does a Pearson correlation coefficient of −0.9 indicate?
explanation: The sign gives the direction and magnitude near 1 a strong linear relationship. Variance explained is r² = 0.81, not 0.9.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Correlation coefficient

question: Y = X² for X symmetric around 0 gives r ≈ 0. What does this show?
options: Pearson r measures only linear association
explanation: A perfect quadratic dependence can have zero linear correlation. Zero r therefore does not imply independence.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Correlation coefficient

question: A simple regression has r = 0.8. What is R²?
explanation: In simple linear regression R² = r² = 0.64, i.e. 64 % of the variance of y is explained by x. The value 0.89 is √0.8.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Correlation coefficient

question: In wage = 1,200 + 2.5 × years of experience, what does 2.5 mean?
options: Each extra year of experience is associated with 2.5 units higher expected wage
explanation: The slope is the expected change in y per one-unit change in x, holding other things equal. It is not a percentage unless y is logged.

source.title: Standard econometrics result without an official EU definition; general background: JRC/OECD Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators (JRC47008)

question: In ln(wage) = a + 0.05 × education (years), what is the approximate interpretation of 0.05?
options: One more year of education is associated with about 5 % higher wage
One more year adds 0.05 to the wage
explanation: In a log-linear model small coefficients approximate proportional changes, so 0.05 ≈ 5 %. A level change of 0.05 would apply to a linear model.

source.title: Standard econometrics result without an official EU definition; general background: JRC/OECD Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators (JRC47008)

question: What is the main consequence of strong multicollinearity among regressors in OLS?
options: Inflated standard errors of the coefficient estimates
explanation: Collinear regressors remain unbiased but individual coefficients become imprecise, shown by high variance inflation factors. R² is not reduced.

source.title: Standard econometrics result without an official EU definition; general background: JRC/OECD Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators (JRC47008)

question: A categorical variable has 4 categories. How many dummy variables enter a regression with an intercept?
explanation: Using all 4 would make the dummies sum to the intercept column (perfect collinearity, the dummy variable trap). Dropping one gives the reference category.

source.title: Standard econometrics result without an official EU definition; general background: JRC/OECD Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators (JRC47008)

question: A dummy for 'female' has coefficient −300 in a wage regression (male is the reference). What does this mean?
options: Women earn 300 less on average than men, other variables held constant
explanation: A dummy coefficient is the difference from the reference group, ceteris paribus. It does not describe an absolute level.

source.title: Standard econometrics result without an official EU definition; general background: JRC/OECD Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators (JRC47008)

question: Residuals fan out as fitted values grow. Which OLS assumption is violated?
explanation: A funnel-shaped residual plot signals heteroscedasticity: coefficients remain unbiased but conventional standard errors are invalid. Robust standard errors are a remedy.

source.title: Standard econometrics result without an official EU definition; general background: JRC/OECD Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators (JRC47008)

question: After adding an irrelevant regressor to an OLS model, what happens?
options: R² cannot fall, but adjusted R² may fall
Both R² and adjusted R² must rise
explanation: R² never decreases when a variable is added, whereas adjusted R² penalises extra parameters. This is why adjusted R² compares models better.

source.title: Standard econometrics result without an official EU definition; general background: JRC/OECD Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators (JRC47008)

question: Wage is regressed on education, but ability (correlated with both) is omitted. What results?
options: Biased estimate of the education coefficient
explanation: An omitted variable correlated with the regressor and affecting the outcome causes omitted variable bias. More data does not remove it.

source.title: Standard econometrics result without an official EU definition; general background: JRC/OECD Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators (JRC47008)

question: A logistic regression coefficient is 0.693. What is the odds ratio per one-unit increase?
explanation: Odds ratio = exp(β) = exp(0.693) ≈ 2, meaning the odds double. The coefficient itself is a change in log-odds.

source.title: Standard econometrics result without an official EU definition; general background: JRC/OECD Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators (JRC47008)

question: Odds of an event are 3 to 1. What is its probability?
explanation: p = odds/(1 + odds) = 3/4 = 0.75. The value 0.33 confuses the odds 3 : 1 with their reciprocal 1/3.

source.title: Standard econometrics result without an official EU definition; general background: JRC/OECD Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators (JRC47008)

question: What is the purpose of splitting data into training and test sets?
options: To estimate performance on unseen data
explanation: Testing on data not used for fitting gives an honest estimate of generalisation error. The AI Act likewise distinguishes training, validation and testing data.

source.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Art. 3(29), (30) and (32) (definitions of training, validation and testing data)

question: A model has 99 % training accuracy but 70 % test accuracy. What is the likely problem?
explanation: A large gap between training and test performance indicates the model memorised noise. Underfitting would show poor performance on both.

source.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Art. 3(30) (validation data used to prevent underfitting or overfitting)

question: In 5-fold cross-validation, how often is each observation used for validation?
explanation: The data are split into 5 folds; each serves once as validation set while the other four train the model. Each observation is used for training four times.

source.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Art. 3(31) (validation data set as a fixed or variable split)

question: Features are standardised using the mean and SD of the full dataset before splitting into train and test. What is this called?
explanation: Test-set information influences preprocessing, making evaluation optimistic. Scaling parameters must be learned on the training data only.

source.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Art. 3(32) (testing data as independent evaluation) and Art. 10(3)

question: Which statement about k-means clustering is correct?
options: It is unaffected by variable scales
The number of clusters k must be chosen in advance
It always finds the global optimum
explanation: K-means is unsupervised, minimises within-cluster distances for a given k, and depends on initialisation and scaling. Unscaled variables with large ranges dominate distances.

source.title: ENISA, Securing Machine Learning Algorithms (2021), general ML background; the tested term is standard ML practice, not defined in EU law

question: Why are fully grown decision trees often problematic?
options: They tend to overfit the training data
explanation: Deep trees fit noise, giving high variance; pruning or depth limits help. Trees handle categories and non-linearity well.

source.title: ENISA, Securing Machine Learning Algorithms (2021), general ML background; the tested term is standard ML practice, not defined in EU law

question: A classifier gives TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 30. What is its precision?
explanation: Precision = TP/(TP + FP) = 40/50 = 0.80. The value 0.67 is recall, 40/60; 0.70 is accuracy.

source.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Art. 15(3) (accuracy and relevant accuracy metrics to be declared)

question: With TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 30, what is the recall (sensitivity)?
explanation: Recall = TP/(TP + FN) = 40/60 ≈ 0.67. The value 0.80 is precision, and 0.75 is specificity.

source.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Art. 15(3) (accuracy and relevant accuracy metrics to be declared)

question: With TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 30, what is the accuracy?
explanation: Accuracy = (TP + TN)/total = 70/100 = 0.70. Precision and recall use only parts of the matrix.

source.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Art. 15(3) (accuracy and relevant accuracy metrics to be declared)

question: With TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 30, what is the specificity?
explanation: Specificity = TN/(TN + FP) = 30/40 = 0.75, the share of true negatives correctly identified. Recall is 0.67.

source.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Art. 15(3) (accuracy and relevant accuracy metrics to be declared)

question: Only 1 % of cases are positive. A classifier predicts 'negative' for everyone. What are its accuracy and recall?
explanation: All negatives are classified correctly (99 %) but no positive is found (recall 0). Accuracy is misleading with imbalanced classes.

source.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Art. 15(3) (accuracy and relevant accuracy metrics to be declared)

question: A classifier has precision 1.0 and recall 0.5. What is its F1 score?
explanation: F1 is the harmonic mean: 2 × 1 × 0.5/1.5 ≈ 0.67. The arithmetic mean (0.75) is not used because the harmonic mean penalises imbalance.

source.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Art. 15(3) (accuracy and relevant accuracy metrics to be declared)

question: What does regularisation such as ridge or lasso do?
options: It penalises large coefficients to reduce overfitting
It increases the number of predictors
It removes the need for a test set
explanation: A penalty term shrinks coefficients, trading some bias for lower variance; lasso can set coefficients exactly to zero. Evaluation on held-out data is still required.

source.title: ENISA, Securing Machine Learning Algorithms (2021), general ML background; the tested term is standard ML practice, not defined in EU law

question: As model complexity increases, what generally happens?
explanation: Flexible models fit the training data better (lower bias) but are more sensitive to sample noise (higher variance). Optimal complexity balances the two.

source.title: ENISA, Securing Machine Learning Algorithms (2021), general ML background; the tested term is standard ML practice, not defined in EU law

question: How does a random forest improve over a single decision tree?
options: It averages many trees built on bootstrap samples, reducing variance
It removes the need for features
explanation: Bagging with random feature subsets decorrelates trees, so averaging reduces variance. Bias remains similar to individual trees.

source.title: ENISA, Securing Machine Learning Algorithms (2021), general ML background; the tested term is standard ML practice, not defined in EU law

question: A binary classifier has a ROC AUC of 0.5. What does this indicate?
options: Accuracy of exactly 50 % on any dataset
A precision of 0.5 at every threshold
Discrimination no better than random guessing
explanation: AUC is the probability that a random positive is ranked above a random negative; 0.5 means no discrimination, 1.0 perfect. It is threshold-independent, so it does not fix accuracy or precision.

source.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Art. 15(3) (accuracy and relevant accuracy metrics to be declared)

question: Which principle is central to effective dashboard design?
options: Show the few key indicators the audience needs, at a glance
Use decorative 3D effects to attract attention
Include every available indicator on one screen
explanation: A dashboard supports monitoring and decisions for a defined audience, so clutter hurts. Metadata and definitions should remain accessible.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Statistical indicator

question: Which feature makes a KPI useful for management?
options: Being measurable only once a year
Being reported in many different units
A clear definition, baseline and target
explanation: A KPI tracks progress towards an objective and needs a precise definition, baseline and target to be interpretable.

source.title: Eurostat Statistics Explained, Glossary: Indicator

question: A choropleth map shows the number of unemployed people by NUTS 2 region. What is the main flaw?
options: The colour scale is too pale
Absolute counts mostly reflect population size; rates should be mapped
Choropleth maps only work with text
explanation: Shading areas by raw counts makes populous regions look like problem regions. Choropleth maps should show normalised values such as rates or per-capita figures.

source.title: Data Visualisation Guide (Publications Office, data.europa.eu), Normalising data for mapping

question: Which colour scheme suits a choropleth map of unemployment rates?
options: A sequential scheme from light to dark
explanation: Ordered, one-directional data call for a sequential palette in which darker means higher. Diverging palettes need a meaningful midpoint.

source.title: Data Visualisation Guide (Publications Office, data.europa.eu), Colour for numerical data: colour scales (sequential vs diverging)

question: On a choropleth map, which classification method places an equal number of regions in each class?
explanation: Quantile classification gives each class the same number of areas, which can hide the actual gaps in values. Equal intervals divide the value range evenly.

source.title: Data Visualisation Guide (Publications Office, data.europa.eu), Choropleth classification methods
